## {.meds-section background-color="#003660"}

::: {.ms-num}
Part 1
:::

::: {.ms-title}
How the model reads your prompt
:::

::: {.mt-rule}
:::

::: {.ms-sub}
LLM vocabulary, and what an AI assistant can and can't see
:::

## LLM vocabulary {.smaller}

::: {.vocab-grid}
::: {.vc}
**LLM**

Large language model: predicts the next piece of text from patterns in its training data
:::
::: {.vc}
**Prompt**

Everything you send the model: your question, pasted data, instructions
:::
::: {.vc}
**Token**

The unit a model reads and writes; a word or part of a word
:::
::: {.vc}
**Context window**

The maximum number of tokens the model can work with at once
:::
::: {.vc}
**System prompt**

Hidden instructions the tool gives the model before your prompt
:::
::: {.vc}
**Hallucination**

Confident output that is false: a made-up function, column or citation
:::
::: {.vc}
**Non-determinism**

The same prompt can give different answers each time you run it
:::
::: {.vc}
**Agent**

A model that can use tools (read files, run code) in a loop toward a goal
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Non-determinism matters for the activity: pairs will get different outputs from the same prompt. That's expected, and it's another reason to verify.
:::

## Tokens: how the model reads text {.smaller .roomy}

Models don't read words or characters. They read **tokens**.

::: {.token-demo}
[The]{.tok}[ squ]{.tok}[irrel]{.tok}[ ran]{.tok}[ up]{.tok}[ the]{.tok}[ oak]{.tok}[ tree]{.tok}[.]{.tok}
:::

::: {.token-caption}
Illustrative split. The exact tokens depend on each model's tokenizer.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Rules of thumb (English text)**

- One token is roughly ¾ of a word
- Common words are one token; rare words, numbers and code split into several
- Tools limit and bill usage in tokens
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Why it matters for data work**

- A pasted CSV costs tokens for **every** value
- `glimpse()` + 5 rows: a few hundred tokens
- A full dataset can fill most of the window, leaving less room for your instructions
:::
:::

## The context window {.smaller .roomy}

The model's **working memory** for one request, measured in tokens. Everything below shares it:

::: {.ctx-bar}
[System prompt]{.ctx-seg .s1}[Attached files]{.ctx-seg .s2}[Chat history]{.ctx-seg .s3}[Your prompt]{.ctx-seg .s4}[Response]{.ctx-seg .s5}
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**What happens as it fills**

- The response has to fit too
- Older messages may be summarized or dropped
- Details buried in a long chat get less attention
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**What to do**

- Send structure, not raw data
- One task per chat; start fresh when it drifts
- Restate key constraints in the new chat
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note}
Window sizes vary widely by model and tool, and change often. Check the docs for the one you use.
:::

## What's in the context window? {.smaller}

The model answers using **only** what's in its context window for this request.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Usually in context**

- Your prompt and the chat so far
- Files or selections your IDE assistant attaches (open editor, `@`-mentioned files)
- Output you paste in (errors, `glimpse()`)
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Usually *not* in context**

- The actual values in your data frame
- Your project's goals, field conventions, data-collection quirks
- What you decided in a different chat
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
Long chats drift. When the model starts forgetting constraints, **start a fresh chat** with a short summary of what matters.
:::

::: {.notes}
Show where your IDE (Positron Assistant, Copilot) shows which files are attached. What gets sent varies by tool and settings, so check yours.
:::

## What the model knows (and doesn't) {.smaller .habits}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**It only knows what's in context**

- It hasn't seen your data unless you show it
- Paste `glimpse()` output, column names, a few sample rows
- Say what the data *is*: source, units, one row = ?
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**It predicts plausible text, not truth**

- Code that runs ≠ code that's correct
- It fills gaps with assumptions, silently
- It tends to agree with your framing, even when it's wrong
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-important}
## Four Tips
1. **Give context**: data, goal, audience
2. **Be specific**: tools, constraints, output format
3. **Iterate in small steps**: one task per prompt, then review
4. **Verify**: run it, check the data, ask for its assumptions
:::

::: {.notes}
Core idea: the model's output is only as good as the context it gets. Everything that follows is a way of supplying better context or checking the output.
:::

## The model tends to agree with you {.smaller}

Models are trained to be helpful, which can tip into **sycophancy**: following your framing even when it's wrong (Sharma et al., 2023).

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Leading prompt**

> "Why is fur color such a strong predictor of how squirrels react to people?"

Assumes the effect exists. You'll likely get an explanation, not a check.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Neutral prompt**

> "Is there evidence in this data that fur color is related to how squirrels react to people? What would make that comparison unreliable?"

Asks for evidence *and* limitations.
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-important}
Ask questions that the data could answer **"no"** to.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Socratic Prompting
The neutral prompt above is an example of **Socratic prompting**. Instead of telling the model what to find, ask it what the evidence would need to look like.
:::

## Anatomy of a good prompt {.smaller}

::: {.prompt-anatomy}
[**Context**]{.pa-tag .pa-context} I'm working with the 2020 NYC Park Squirrel Census in R. One row = one squirrel sighting. Columns include fur color, location, height and free-text activities.

[**Task**]{.pa-tag .pa-task} Write a cleaning script for the activities column.

[**Constraints**]{.pa-tag .pa-constraints} Use tidyverse. Don't drop or overwrite any original values; put derived columns next to the originals.

[**Output**]{.pa-tag .pa-output} One R chunk, then a list of every value you couldn't parse.

[**Check**]{.pa-tag .pa-check} Before writing code, list your assumptions and ask me about anything ambiguous.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
Context doesn't have to live in every prompt. Recall from our last workshop that a **system prompt** or **project pre prompt** can carry context so you don't have to repeat it each time. 
:::

::: {.notes}
Five parts. Not every prompt needs all five, but the first one (context) and the last one (check) are the ones people skip.
:::

## Prompting fundamentals {.smaller .fund}

| Fundamental | Weak prompt | Stronger prompt |
|---|---|---|
| **Context** | "Clean this data" | "This is the 2020 NYC Park Squirrel Census, one row per squirrel sighting" |
| **Role / audience** | *(none)* | "I'm a data manager preparing this for a public archive" |
| **Task + constraints** | "Make a plot" | "Use ggplot2, colorblind-safe palette, one plot per park" |
| **Output format** | *Not specifying* | "Return a single R chunk plus 3 bullet caveats" |
| **Surface assumptions** | *(none)* | "Before writing code, list your assumptions about each column" |
| **Invite pushback** | *(none)* | "If my approach is flawed, say so before writing code" |

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
## The last two rows matter most
Models fill gaps silently. Asking for assumptions and pushback is how you catch data loss **before** it happens.
:::

## Show the model your data (safely)

The model can't see your data frame. Give it the **structure**, not the whole dataset.

```{r}
dplyr::glimpse(squirrels)          # column names, types, first values
head(squirrels, 5) |> knitr::kable() # a few example rows
dput(head(squirrels, 5))           # reproducible snippet it can run
```

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Do**

- Paste schema + a few rows
- Describe units and how the data was collected
- Mention known messiness
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Don't**

- Paste sensitive or restricted data into tools your institution hasn't approved
- Assume the model knows your column meanings
:::
:::

## Iterate in small steps

::: {.loop}
[1 · Plan]{.loop-step} → [2 · Code one step]{.loop-step} → [3 · Run]{.loop-step} → [4 · Review]{.loop-step} → [repeat]{.loop-step .loop-repeat}
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Instead of…**

> "Clean the data, fit a model and make five plots."

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Try…**

> "First, propose a plan in 4–6 steps. Don't write code yet."

:::
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
Each step should be small enough that **you** can check it.
:::

## Verify before you trust {.smaller}

AI-written cleaning code can **run perfectly and still lose data**. Check it.

```{r}
n_before <- nrow(squirrels)
clean    <- clean_squirrels(squirrels)   # AI-written function

stopifnot(nrow(clean) == n_before)       # no rows silently dropped

# how many new NAs did cleaning create in a column?
na_added <- function(before, after, col) {
  sum(is.na(after[[col]])) - sum(is.na(before[[col]]))
}
```

**Prompts that help**

- *"Which values does this code turn into NA?"*
- *"Write tests that would fail if this code dropped data."*
- *"Explain this function line by line."*

## Does being *mean* help? {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Dobariya & Kumar (2025), *Mind Your Tone***

- 50 multiple-choice questions (math, science, history)
- Each rewritten in 5 tones → **250 prompts**
- Model: ChatGPT-4o

| Tone | Accuracy |
|---|---|
| Very polite | ~80.8% |
| Very rude | ~84.8% |

Rude prompts scored ~4 points higher.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
**Before you start insulting Copilot…**

- One model, one version, 50 questions
- Multiple choice ≠ writing your analysis code
- Earlier work (Yin et al., 2024) found **impolite prompts often hurt** performance on older models
- Open question: is it rudeness, or that rude prompts are **shorter and more direct**?

:::
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-note}
**Takeaway:** Tone is a variable. Directness beats deference. Hostility isn't the skill — *clarity* is.
:::

::: {.notes}
Good discussion prompt: how would you design a study to separate "rude" from "concise"? This is a reproducibility lesson too: a single-model, single-run result is a hypothesis, not a rule.
:::

## Meet the data: NYC park squirrels {.smaller}

::: {.squirrel-stats}
::: {.stat}
[72]{.stat-num}
[volunteer "Squirrel Sighters"]{.stat-label}
:::
::: {.stat}
[433]{.stat-num}
[squirrel sightings]{.stat-label}
:::
::: {.stat}
[24]{.stat-num}
[parks in Manhattan and Brooklyn]{.stat-label}
:::
:::

- **2020 Park Squirrel Census:** counted on a single afternoon in early March 2020
- Two linked tables: one row per **squirrel** sighting, one row per **park** (conditions, litter, other animals)
- Records fur color, location, height above ground, activities and reactions to humans
- Real-world messy: free-text notes, inconsistent heights, values like "'Cool' - Hank"

::: {.footer-note}
Source: The Squirrel Census / NYC Open Data, *2020 Park Squirrel Census*
:::

## Same data, three roles {.roles}

**2020 Park Squirrel Census** (433 sightings, 24 parks) · "I am [role]. Clean this dataset for me."

Different roles yielded different methods to to clean the data. 

The four methods used were: 

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- **Preserved:** script left the data intact without removing anything
- **Transformed:**  values were simplified or normalized, but original meaning kept
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- **Interpreted:**  data changed shape (e.g. one column split into many), steering it toward a specific analysis
- **Discarded:** values present in the raw data were silently dropped
:::
:::



## What each role did to the data {.smaller}

```{=html}
<div class="role-grid">
  <div class="rg-legend">
    <span><i class="dot preserved"></i>preserved</span>
    <span><i class="dot transformed"></i>transformed</span>
    <span><i class="dot interpreted"></i>interpreted</span>
    <span><i class="dot discarded"></i>discarded</span>
  </div>

  <div class="rg-label">Height: corrupted ranges<br>(e.g. '6–18')</div>
  <div class="rg-cell discarded fragment" data-fragment-index="1">Coerced to NA (data lost)</div>
  <div class="rg-cell transformed fragment" data-fragment-index="2">Fixed encoding → kept as '6-18'</div>
  <div class="rg-cell interpreted fragment" data-fragment-index="3">Extracted lower bound → numeric 6</div>

  <div class="rg-label">Activities column<br>(e.g. 'Foraging, Running')</div>
  <div class="rg-cell preserved fragment" data-fragment-index="1">Kept as-is</div>
  <div class="rg-cell preserved fragment" data-fragment-index="2">Kept as-is</div>
  <div class="rg-cell interpreted fragment" data-fragment-index="3">Split into 7 TRUE/FALSE cols, dropped original</div>

  <div class="rg-label">Park conditions<br>(e.g. 'Calm, pick-up game')</div>
  <div class="rg-cell transformed fragment" data-fragment-index="1">Extracted core category + saved note separately</div>
  <div class="rg-cell transformed fragment" data-fragment-index="2">Extracted first word only</div>
  <div class="rg-cell interpreted fragment" data-fragment-index="3">Hard-coded 3 categories; anything else → NA</div>

  <div class="rg-label">Unusual value<br>("'Cool' - Hank")</div>
  <div class="rg-cell preserved fragment" data-fragment-index="1">Preserved as 'Cool'</div>
  <div class="rg-cell discarded fragment" data-fragment-index="2">Silently dropped → NA</div>
  <div class="rg-cell discarded fragment" data-fragment-index="3">Silently dropped → NA</div>

  <div class="rg-label">Extra detail in text<br>(e.g. 'Some, in trees')</div>
  <div class="rg-cell preserved fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><span>Kept in separate <em>_notes</em> column</span></div>
  <div class="rg-cell discarded fragment" data-fragment-index="2">Discarded</div>
  <div class="rg-cell discarded fragment" data-fragment-index="3">Discarded</div>

  <div></div>

</div>
```

::: {.footer-note}
Adapted from A. Dillman, *Yes, And… AI in Your IDE*, posit::conf(2026)
:::

::: {.notes}
Advance three times: data manager, then data science student, then environmental researcher. Same prompt, same data. The role decided what survived.
:::

## What the squirrels taught us {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**What happened**

- Same prompt, same data → **three different datasets**
- Each role's choices were reasonable *for that role*
- The worst losses were **silent**: values became NA with no warning
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**How to prevent it**

- State your goal *and* what must be preserved
- Ask for a list of every value that was changed or dropped
- Compare row counts and NA counts before and after
- Keep original columns; add derived ones beside them
:::
:::

. . .


## Activity: Prompt makeover

**Goal:** turn a weak prompt into a strong one, and *measure* the difference.

**Task:** create a numeric height column from the squirrel census's messy height values (ranges like '6–18', free text, blanks).

::: {.round-grid}
::: {.round}
[Round 1 · 3 min]{.round-tag}

**Weak prompt**

Baseline: see what you get
:::
::: {.round}
[Round 2 · 5 min]{.round-tag .r2}

**Add context + constraints**

Objective 1: write a complete prompt
:::
::: {.round}
[Round 3 · 5 min]{.round-tag .r3}

**Assumptions first**

Objective 2: make the model show its assumptions
:::
::: {.round}
[Round 4 · 5 min]{.round-tag .r4}

**Verify**

Objective 3: check the code against the data
:::
:::

[Pairs · ~20 minutes · start a **fresh chat** for each round · use **claude.ai** in your browser or the Claude desktop app]{.activity-time}

::: {.notes}
Pairs: one person types, one keeps score. Fresh chat each round so earlier rounds don't leak context. Download activity-starter.R before starting.
:::

## The prompts {.act-prompts .smaller}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Setup

Do this before Round 1:

1. **Download the2020 Park Squirrel Census: Squirrel Data** from [thesquirrelcensus.com/data](https://www.thesquirrelcensus.com/data)
2. **Download `activity-starter.R`** from the workshop page at [ucsb-meds.github.io/AI-for-EDS](https://ucsb-meds.github.io/AI-for-EDS)
3. **Open `activity-starter.R`** in RStudio or Positron — it loads the data and defines `check_cleaning()`
4. Update the file path at the top to point to your downloaded CSV, then run the setup chunk
5. **Open [claude.ai](https://claude.ai) in your browser** (or the Claude desktop app). 

You're ready when `glimpse(squirrels)` runs without error.

### Round 1

**Steps:**

1. In R, run `dplyr::glimpse(squirrels)` and copy the output
2. Start a **fresh chat** in Claude
3. Paste the following prompt into Claude: 
> Here is my data: **[paste glimpse() output.]** Clean the `above_ground_height_in_feet` column.
4. Paste Claude's code into the `clean_r1` variable assignment section of `activity-starter.R` and run it
5. Fill in your Round 1 scorecard row based on the output


### Round 2

**Steps:**

1. Start a **fresh chat**
2. Run `dplyr::glimpse(squirrels)` and copy the output
3. Paste the following prompt into Claude:

> I'm analyzing the 2020 NYC Park Squirrel Census in R with the tidyverse. One row = one squirrel sighting. Here is the `glimpse()` output: **[paste]**
>
> The `above_ground_height_in_feet` column records how far above ground each squirrel was observed, but values are messy — some are ranges (e.g. '6–18'), some are text, some are blank.
>
> Write code that adds a **new** numeric column. **Keep the original column unchanged.** Return one R chunk.

4. Paste Claude's code into the `clean_r2` variable assignment section of `activity-starter.R` and run it
5. Fill in your Round 2 scorecard row


### Round 3

**Steps:**

1. Start a **fresh chat**
2. Send the Round 2 prompt plus the addition below

  > Prompt: **Round 2 prompt +:**

> **Before writing any code**, list every distinct kind of value in the `above_ground_height_in_feet` column, how you plan to convert each one, and anything you're unsure about. Wait for my answer.

3. Read the model's list of assumptions and answer any questions it asks before it writes code (e.g. *"For ranges like '6–18', should I take the lower bound, upper bound, or midpoint?"*)
4. Once you've answered, tell Claude: *"Now write the code."*
5. Paste Claude's code into the `clean_r3` variable assignment section of `activity-starter.R` and run it
6. Fill in your Round 3 scorecard row



### Round 4

**Steps:**

1. In `activity-starter.R`, run the check on your Round 1 and Round 3 outputs, using  the cleaned data frame:

```{r}
check_cleaning(squirrels, clean_r1, height_col)
check_cleaning(squirrels, clean_r3, height_col)
```

2. Compare the two outputs. Which round created more NAs?
3. Back in Claude, ask: *"Which values in `above_ground_height_in_feet` does your code turn into NA? List them."*
4. Does its answer match what `check_cleaning()` showed?
5. Fill in the Round 4 column on your scorecard

:::


## Verify: the check function {.smaller}

In `activity-starter.R`, and worth keeping for any AI-written cleaning code:

```{r}
check_cleaning <- function(before, after, col) {
  if (!col %in% names(after)) stop("Column '", col, "' was renamed or dropped")
  tibble::tibble(
    rows_before   = nrow(before),
    rows_after    = nrow(after),
    na_before     = sum(is.na(before[[col]])),
    na_after      = sum(is.na(after[[col]])),
    values_before = dplyr::n_distinct(before[[col]]),
    values_after  = dplyr::n_distinct(after[[col]])
  )
}
```

::: {.callout-tip}
If `na_after > na_before`, the code turned real observations into missing data. Did the model warn you?
:::

## Scorecard + debrief {.scorecard}

| | Round 1 | Round 2 | Round 3 |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| Rows kept? | | | |
| Original column kept? | | | |
| New NAs created | | | |
| Model told you what it changed? | | | |
| Code you'd actually use? | | | |

. . .

::: {.callout-note}
## Debrief (5 min)
1. Which round lost the least data, and **which fundamental** made the difference?
2. In Round 4, did the model's own answer match the check?
3. What will you add to your prompts from now on?
:::

## {.meds-section background-color="#003660"}

::: {.ms-num}
Part 4
:::

::: {.ms-title}
From prompts to agents
:::

::: {.mt-rule}
:::

::: {.ms-sub}
Write it down once: agentic coding and skills
:::

## You just did the same work four times

In the activity, every round you:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- pasted the same `glimpse()` output
- retyped "keep the original column"
- copied code from chat into R
- ran the check yourself
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-important}
## Two questions
1. What if the assistant could **run the code and the check itself**?
2. What if you wrote your context and rules **once**, and it reused them every time?
:::
:::
:::

. . .

That's **agentic coding** (1) and **skills** (2).

## Chat assistant vs. coding agent

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.mode-card}
**Chat assistant**

1. You write a prompt
2. It suggests code
3. **You** copy, run and check it
4. **You** paste back errors

You run the loop.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.mode-card .agent}
**Coding agent** (e.g. Claude Code)

1. You describe the goal
2. It reads your files and data
3. It writes code, **runs it**, sees errors, fixes them
4. You review and approve changes

It runs the loop. **You stay the reviewer.**
:::
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip}
An agent can act on your files, so the fundamentals matter **more**, not less.
:::

## Same fundamentals, new home {.smaller .map}

| Fundamental | In a chat | In Claude Code |
|---|---|---|
| **Context** | Paste `glimpse()` every time | It reads your repo; project notes live in `CLAUDE.md` |
| **Be specific** | Retype constraints | Write rules once in a **skill** |
| **Small steps** | "Do step 1 only" | Ask for a plan first, approve it, then let it work |
| **Surface assumptions** | "List your assumptions" | Built into the skill: *before writing code…* |
| **Verify** | You run the check | It runs the check script; you review the diff |

## What is a skill? {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
A **skill** is a folder with a `SKILL.md` file: written instructions Claude follows for a specific kind of task.

- **Frontmatter:** a `name` and a `description` of when to use it
- **Body:** the steps and rules, in plain Markdown
- Claude sees every skill's description, and loads the full instructions **only when a task matches**
- Or run one yourself: `/safe-data-cleaning`
- Can bundle scripts, like our check function
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
```text
my-project/
└── .claude/
    └── skills/
        └── safe-data-cleaning/
            ├── SKILL.md
            └── scripts/
                └── check_cleaning.R
```

Project skills live in `.claude/skills/` and are shared through git. Personal ones go in `~/.claude/skills/`.
:::
:::

## Today's prompts, as a skill {.smaller .skill-slide}

```markdown
---
name: safe-data-cleaning
description: >
  Clean or recode a column in an environmental dataset
  without losing data. Use when asked to clean, tidy,
  recode or parse a column.
---

## Before writing code
1. Run `glimpse()` and `count()` on the target column.
2. List each kind of value and how you'll convert it.
3. Ask about anything ambiguous; wait for my answers.

## Rules
- Never overwrite or drop original columns; add new ones.
- Never drop rows. Use the tidyverse.

## After writing code
- Run `scripts/check_cleaning.R`; report rows and NAs.
- List every original value that became NA.
```

::: {.footer-note}
Rounds 2–4 of the activity, written down once. It's in this repo at `.claude/skills/safe-data-cleaning/`.
:::

## Key takeaways {.smaller}

::: {.takeaway-grid}
::: {.tk}
[1]{.tk-num}
**Context is everything.** The model only knows what you show it.
:::
::: {.tk}
[2]{.tk-num}
**Be specific.** Tools, constraints, output format.
:::
::: {.tk}
[3]{.tk-num}
**Go step by step.** Plan first, then one task at a time.
:::
::: {.tk}
[4]{.tk-num}
**Ask neutral questions.** Let the data say "no."
:::
::: {.tk}
[5]{.tk-num}
**Surface assumptions.** Ask what it changed or dropped.
:::
::: {.tk}
[6]{.tk-num}
**Verify.** Row counts, NA counts, tests. You're the scientist.
:::
:::
